stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. A new instance needs several minutes to start before it can serve requests. Traffic follows a predictable pattern: it rises to a peak from 09:00 to 11:00 every weekday. Users must not see slow responses during a rise in traffic that can be anticipated. A few minutes of slow responses are acceptable during a rise that cannot be anticipated. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Add a target tracking scaling policy that keeps the average CPU utilization of the group near a target value, with no scheduled actions.
options.why: Target tracking is dynamic scaling, [which is reactive in nature](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-long-initialization-fit): the instances start minutes after the 09:00 rise, and users see slow responses.
options.misconception: expects a metric-based policy to add capacity before a known peak arrives

options.text: Add scheduled actions that raise the minimum capacity before 09:00 and lower it after 11:00 on weekdays, and add a target tracking scaling policy.
options.why: You can [use scheduled scaling and scaling policies together](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-plus-policies-together): the raised minimum is in place before the peak, and target tracking removes capacity after 11:00.

options.text: Add a predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode that adds and removes instances from its forecast, with no other scaling policy.
options.why: Predictive scaling launches early, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in), so a policy that removes instances from its forecast does not exist.

options.text: Set the minimum, maximum and desired capacity of the group to the number of instances that the highest daily peak needs.
options.why: It works, but the group pays for the peak capacity outside 09:00 to 11:00 as well, which costs more than scheduled actions.

explanation: The peak is known, and a new instance needs minutes to start, so the capacity is needed before 09:00. Scheduled scaling fits when [the need arises on a predictable schedule](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use). A scheduled action sets [desired, minimum, and maximum capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-action-sets-capacities) at a set time, and target tracking then follows the load inside those limits.
takeaway: A known peak and slow-starting instances: raise capacity with a scheduled action, and let target tracking follow the rest.
twin: If the stem said "Traffic rises to a peak several times a day at unpredictable times, with no daily or weekly pattern" instead: target tracking alone, because dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).
say: The peak is on a schedule, so I'd raise the minimum before nine and let target tracking handle the rest.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon ECS. The application stores orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table that uses provisioned capacity mode. During sales events, the number of requests grows quickly and then falls again. The company wants the number of ECS tasks and the read and write capacity of the table to follow the load automatically. Which AWS service should a solutions architect use to scale both resources?
keywords: read and write capacity of the table

options.text: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, with an Auto Scaling group whose scaling policy adds ECS tasks and DynamoDB table capacity
options.why: EC2 Auto Scaling is the choice when you [only need to scale Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-use-ec2-vs-aws-auto-scaling) groups; tasks and table capacity are not instances in a group.

options.text: Application Auto Scaling, with a target tracking scaling policy for the ECS service and another one for the DynamoDB table
options.why: Application Auto Scaling scales resources other than EC2 instances, and it supports [target tracking scaling](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-aas-policy-types) for the ECS service and for the table.

options.text: Elastic Load Balancing, with an Application Load Balancer that spreads the growing number of requests across the ECS tasks
options.why: A load balancer [automatically distributes your incoming traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-what-distributes-traffic-across-targets) across targets, but it adds no tasks and no table capacity.
options.misconception: believes that spreading requests adds capacity

options.text: AWS Auto Scaling, with a scaling plan that creates step scaling policies for the ECS service and the DynamoDB table
options.why: A scaling plan creates [target tracking scaling policies only](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-faq-creates-target-tracking-only), so the step scaling policies in this option cannot come from it.
options.misconception: believes that a scaling plan creates any type of scaling policy

explanation: An ECS service and a DynamoDB table are not EC2 instances. For resources like these, [you can use the Application Auto Scaling API](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-faq-application-auto-scaling-for-non-ec2). An ECS service supports [auto scaling of its task count](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-aas-scalable-dimension-examples), and a table in provisioned mode scales [the read and write capacity of the table](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-aas-scalable-dimension-examples).
takeaway: EC2 instances scale with EC2 Auto Scaling; ECS tasks and DynamoDB capacity scale with Application Auto Scaling.
twin: If the stem said "a fleet of EC2 instances" instead: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, because for instances you [use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-wa-ec2-auto-scaling-for-instances-application-auto-scaling-for-other-services).
say: ECS tasks and DynamoDB capacity aren't EC2, so I'd use Application Auto Scaling for both.

stem: A company uses an Amazon SQS queue to decouple its web tier from an image-processing tier. Worker instances in an Auto Scaling group poll the queue. One worker needs about 2 seconds to process one message, and each message must be processed within 60 seconds after it arrives. The number of uploaded images changes a lot during the day, so the processing tier must be scalable. Which scaling configuration will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: about 2 seconds to process one message

options.text: A target tracking scaling policy on the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric of the queue, with a target value of 30 messages
options.why: The queue length [might not change proportionally](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-queue-length-not-proportional) to the size of the group, so the policy adds the wrong number of workers.

options.text: A target tracking scaling policy on the average CPU utilization of the worker group, with a target value of 50 percent
options.why: For queue work, AWS says [100% CPU utilization is expected and should not be your primary metric](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-queue-depth-metric-for-batch-work); the queue shows the waiting work.
options.misconception: treats CPU utilization as the measure of queued work

options.text: A fixed group size that matches the number of workers needed at the highest daily upload rate, with no scaling policy
options.why: It works, but the group pays for peak workers all day; when uploads change, AWS says [you might consider using dynamic scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-dynamic-scaling-when-load-varies).

options.text: A target tracking scaling policy on metric math that divides ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible by GroupInServiceInstances, with a target value of 30
options.why: The metric falls as workers are added, so target tracking adds workers when the backlog grows and removes them when it shrinks.

explanation: One worker clears a message in 2 seconds, and a message can wait 60 seconds, so one worker can hold a backlog of 30. AWS says to take the acceptable latency and [divide it by the average time](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-acceptable-backlog-per-instance-target) per message. The metric is the [backlog per instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance): [ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math) divided by GroupInServiceInstances, which metric math calculates.
takeaway: Scale queue workers on backlog per instance; the target is the acceptable latency divided by the time per message.
twin: If the stem said "about 6 seconds to process one message" instead: the same metric with a target of 10, because you take the latency and [divide it by the average time](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-acceptable-backlog-per-instance-target).
say: I'd scale the workers on backlog per instance, with a target of thirty messages per worker.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The security team has built a new, patched AMI. Every running instance must be replaced with an instance from the new AMI, and at least 90% of the desired capacity must stay in service during the change. The company follows an immutable infrastructure model and does not patch instances in place. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Every running instance must be replaced
at least 90% of the desired capacity

options.text: Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and wait for the group to update the running instances.
options.why: A new version changes later launches only: running instances stay, and new or replacement instances use the [current settings of the Auto Scaling group](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-replacement-uses-current-settings).

options.text: Edit the launch configuration of the group so that it names the new AMI, and let the group apply the edit to the running instances.
options.why: You [can't modify a launch configuration](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-immutable) after you create it, so the edit in this option is not possible.

options.text: Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and start an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 90%.
options.why: The refresh replaces every running instance with one from the new version and keeps 90% of the desired capacity in service while it works.

options.text: Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and terminate the old instances by hand, a few at a time.
options.why: It works, but someone terminates and watches each batch by hand, while an instance refresh does the same work as one managed operation.

explanation: An instance refresh is the managed way to replace running instances, for example when [deploying a new Amazon Machine Image (AMI)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-instance-refresh-use-cases). Its minimum healthy percentage is the share of [the desired capacity to keep in service](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-instance-refresh-min-max-healthy), so a value of 90% matches the stem. Each instance is replaced, not patched, which keeps the model immutable.
takeaway: A new launch template version changes future launches; an instance refresh replaces the instances that already run.
twin: If the stem said "all instances can be replaced at the same time" instead: an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of [0 percent](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-instance-refresh-all-at-once).
say: I'd add a template version with the new AMI and start an instance refresh.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: every running instance moves to the new AMI, at least 90% of the capacity stays in service, and nothing is patched in place, because the model is immutable.
Before I look at the options, I predict a new launch template version plus an instance refresh, because a new version alone changes only the instances that launch later.

I remove the edit of the launch configuration, because a launch configuration cannot be modified after it is created. I remove the option that only waits, because the running instances keep their old AMI.

Between the instance refresh and terminating the old instances by hand the difference is who does the work; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, so the managed refresh wins, and its minimum healthy percentage keeps 90% in service.
Check: the instance refresh replaces every instance, keeps 90% of the capacity in service and changes nothing in place. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company runs stateless video-encoding workers on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The workers take jobs from a queue, and the jobs can tolerate interruption and can be restarted. At least two workers must keep running even if Amazon EC2 reclaims Spot capacity. The number of other workers changes with the number of jobs. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: At least two workers must keep running

options.text: Use a mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base capacity of 2 instances, and use Spot Instances for all capacity above the base.
options.why: Anything above the base can run on Spot, or on a [specified percentage mix of On-Demand or Spot instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-on-demand-base-spot-above); here the mix is all Spot.

options.text: Run every worker as an On-Demand Instance, and scale the group with a target tracking policy on the backlog per instance.
options.why: It works, but Spot Instances cost [up to 90%](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-discount-up-to-90-percent) less than On-Demand prices, and these jobs can be restarted.

options.text: Specify one instance type in the mixed instances policy, and use the lowest-price allocation strategy for the Spot Instances.
options.why: The lowest-price strategy has the [highest risk of interruption](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-lowest-price-not-recommended), and one instance type gives Spot fewer pools to choose from.

options.text: Specify several instance types in the mixed instances policy, and use the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy for the Spot Instances.
options.why: Several instance types give Spot more pools, and this strategy picks pools that are [least likely to be interrupted](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-price-capacity-optimized-recommended) at a low price.

options.text: Run every worker as a Spot Instance, and turn on instance scale-in protection so that Amazon EC2 does not reclaim two of the workers.
options.why: Spot interruptions [bypass all Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling protection mechanisms](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-interruption-bypasses-all-protection), so scale-in protection keeps no worker running.

explanation: AWS lets the [base capacity be fulfilled with On-Demand instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-on-demand-base-spot-above), so two workers stay out of Spot, and the rest runs on Spot. For Spot, be [flexible about which instance types you request](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-be-flexible-types-and-azs), and use the [price and capacity optimized allocation strategy](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-price-capacity-optimized-recommended) that AWS recommends.
takeaway: Keep the required minimum on an On-Demand base, run the rest on Spot, and diversify the instance types.
twin: If the stem said "the jobs cannot be restarted" instead: On-Demand Instances, because Spot does not suit work that is [inflexible, stateful, fault-intolerant, or tightly coupled](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-not-suitable-stateful-inflexible).
say: An On-Demand base of two, Spot above it, and several instance types with price-capacity-optimized.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. A new instance needs several minutes to start before it can serve requests. Traffic rises to a peak several times a day at unpredictable times, with no daily or weekly pattern. Users must not see slow responses during a rise in traffic that can be anticipated. A few minutes of slow responses are acceptable during a rise that cannot be anticipated. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: A few minutes of slow responses are acceptable

options.text: Add a target tracking scaling policy that keeps the average CPU utilization of the group near a target value, with no scheduled actions.
options.why: It adds instances when the metric rises and removes them afterwards, [scaling in more gradually when traffic is decreasing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-target-tracking-scale-in-gradual), so idle capacity stays small.

options.text: Add scheduled actions that raise the minimum capacity before 09:00 and lower it after 11:00 on weekdays, and add a target tracking scaling policy.
options.why: It works, but the raised weekday minimum pays for extra instances that the stem gives no reason for, because the peaks follow no schedule.

options.text: Add a predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode that adds and removes instances from its forecast, with no other scaling policy.
options.why: [Predictive scaling uses patterns to scale out](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-predictive-patterns-vs-scheduled-times), and [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in), so it fits neither this traffic nor the claim in the option.

options.text: Set the minimum, maximum and desired capacity of the group to the number of instances that the highest daily peak needs.
options.why: It works, but the group runs the peak number of instances all day, although the stem accepts a few minutes of slow responses.

explanation: The peaks have no pattern, so no setting can add instances before them, and the stem accepts a few minutes of slow responses. Target tracking [adjusts the number of EC2 instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-target-tracking-definition) to hold a target, so it follows each peak up and down. Dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).
takeaway: Peaks at unknown times: use target tracking, which reacts to the load and scales in after it.
twin: If the stem said "Traffic follows a predictable pattern: it rises to a peak from 09:00 to 11:00 every weekday" instead: scheduled actions plus target tracking, because you can [use scheduled scaling and scaling policies together](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-plus-policies-together).
say: There's no pattern to plan for, so target tracking alone is the cheapest fit.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The load balancer is enabled in Availability Zone A and Availability Zone B. The Auto Scaling group has one subnet, in Availability Zone A, so every instance runs in that zone. The company needs the web tier to be highly available across multiple Availability Zones. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: enabled in Availability Zone A and Availability Zone B
has one subnet, in Availability Zone A

options.text: Add a subnet in Availability Zone B to the Auto Scaling group, so that the group places its instances in both zones.
options.why: The [desired capacity is distributed across these Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-desired-spread-across-azs), and the load balancer already sends traffic to zone B.

options.text: Add a subnet in Availability Zone C to the Auto Scaling group, and keep the load balancer enabled in zones A and B.
options.why: The load balancer is not enabled in zone C, and for registered targets in such a zone it [does not route traffic to them](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lb-no-traffic-to-disabled-az).

options.text: Extend the Auto Scaling group into a second AWS Region, and register the new instances with the same load balancer.
options.why: Auto Scaling groups are Regional: they [can span Availability Zones, but not AWS regions](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-regional-spans-azs-not-regions).

options.text: Create a second Auto Scaling group with a subnet in Availability Zone B, and attach it to the same target group.
options.why: It works, but two groups mean two sets of scaling policies and settings to keep in step, and one group can use both zones.

explanation: Instances in one zone share that zone's fate: if it fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances). AWS recommends a group [across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-resilience-practices) with the load balancer in the same zones. Zone B is already enabled on the load balancer, so one more subnet in the group completes the design.
takeaway: For high availability, give one Auto Scaling group subnets in several zones that the load balancer also uses.
twin: If the stem said "keep running if the whole Region fails" instead: a second group in another Region, because groups are [regional constructs](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-regional-spans-azs-not-regions).
say: Add a zone B subnet to the group; the load balancer already serves zone B.

stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Traffic follows a predictable daily pattern with a peak every morning. The group has one predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode and no other scaling policy. The instances are ready before each morning peak, but the group keeps its peak capacity through the night, and the monthly cost has grown. The application must stay ready for the morning peak. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: keeps its peak capacity through the night

options.text: Switch the predictive scaling policy to forecast only mode, so that the policy removes the extra instances when the forecast falls.
options.why: In [forecast only](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-forecast-only-mode-first) mode the policy forecasts capacity but does not scale the group, so it removes nothing and also stops the morning scale-out.

options.text: Add a scheduled action each evening that sets the desired capacity to the night level, and keep the predictive scaling policy.
options.why: It works, but capacity stays at the peak level from the end of the morning peak until the evening action, which costs more than following the load.

options.text: Add a target tracking scaling policy on average CPU utilization, and keep the predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode.
options.why: Target tracking removes instances when the metric falls below the target, and the predictive policy keeps [launching capacity in advance of forecasted load](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-long-initialization-fit).

options.text: Let predictive scaling raise and lower the maximum capacity of the group automatically when the forecast changes.
options.why: A maximum that predictive scaling raised [does not automatically decrease back](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-raised-max-stays) to the original value, so this setting cannot lower it.
options.misconception: believes that predictive scaling lowers the maximum capacity again after it raised it

explanation: Predictive scaling adds instances ahead of the forecast, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in). You can [combine predictive scaling and dynamic scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-combine-policy-types-predictive-plus-dynamic): the predictive policy keeps the mornings ready, and the target tracking policy removes instances when the load falls.
takeaway: Pair predictive scaling with target tracking: predictive scaling adds capacity early, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in).
twin: If the stem said "traffic has no daily or weekly pattern" instead: target tracking without the predictive policy, because dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).
say: Predictive scaling only scales out, so I'd add target tracking to bring capacity down at night.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the change that is MOST cost-effective.
I mark the constraints: one predictive policy in forecast and scale mode, the mornings must stay ready, and capacity stays at the peak level through the night.
Before I look at the options, I predict forecast only mode, because I think that mode lets the forecast remove the extra instances at night.
I remove the option that raises and lowers the maximum automatically, because a maximum that predictive scaling raised does not go back down automatically.

Between forecast only mode and a target tracking policy the difference is what scales in. My first idea breaks because forecast only mode does not scale the group at all, in either direction, and predictive scaling does not scale in. So the group needs a dynamic policy, and target tracking follows the load, which costs less than a fixed evening action.
Check: target tracking plus the predictive policy keeps the mornings ready and removes capacity at night. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. When the group launches an instance, a user data script downloads configuration files for several minutes. The load balancer sends requests to new instances before the script finishes, and users see errors. The company must ensure that no new instance receives traffic before its script ends, and the solution must work automatically for every new instance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: no new instance receives traffic before its script ends

options.text: Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group so that it covers the minutes that the user data script needs.
options.why: The grace period is the [minimum amount of time (in seconds)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-definition) before the group can terminate a new unhealthy instance; it does not delay registration.

options.text: Turn on slow start for the target group so that each new instance receives a small share of the requests while the script runs.
options.why: Slow start still sends requests to the new instance, a smaller share at first, so some users still see errors.
options.misconception: believes that slow start keeps requests away from an instance that is not ready

options.text: Detach the target group from the Auto Scaling group, and use an AWS Lambda function to register each instance after its script reports success.
options.why: It works, but the team writes and runs custom registration code for a pause that a lifecycle hook gives as a group feature.

options.text: Add a launch lifecycle hook to the Auto Scaling group, and make the user data script call CompleteLifecycleAction after the files are in place.
options.why: The script ends the wait itself: you [add the CompleteLifecycleAction API call](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-user-data-complete) to user data, and then the group registers the instance.

explanation: The group [registers your instance with the load balancer](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-registers-with-lb-before-inservice) as the last step before InService. A launch hook holds the new instance in [Pending:Wait](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-hook-states) before that step, so registration waits until the script reports that the application is [ready to accept traffic](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-lb-registration).
takeaway: To keep traffic away until setup ends, use a launch lifecycle hook, not the health check grace period.
twin: If the stem said "logs must be copied to Amazon S3 before scale in removes an instance" instead: a termination lifecycle hook, which [pauses the instance before it is terminated](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-scale-in-use).
say: A launch lifecycle hook holds the instance until the script finishes, so it gets no traffic early.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application keeps user session data in the memory of each instance. When the group scales in, the users on the terminated instances are signed out. The company needs a scalable, stateless web tier that keeps scaling in and out without signing users out. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: session data in the memory of each instance

options.text: Configure the Auto Scaling group to copy the session data of the running instances to every new instance when it launches.
options.why: [Data is not automatically copied](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-data-not-copied-to-new-instances) to new instances, and a copy at launch does not save the sessions of the instance that terminates.

options.text: Change the application to store the session data in an Amazon DynamoDB table that every instance in the group reads and writes.
options.why: A DynamoDB table is a managed store that every instance reads, so the group can remove any instance and the user stays signed in.

options.text: Turn on sticky sessions for the target group so that each user returns to the instance that holds the user's session data.
options.why: Sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), but the session still lives on that instance and is lost at scale in.

options.text: Change the application to store the session data in a cache that the team installs and runs on a separate group of EC2 instances.
options.why: It works, but the team patches, scales and repairs its own cache instances, which is more operational work than a managed table.

explanation: Session data in the memory of an instance goes away with the instance. Well-Architected says to offload session data to a [database, cache, or external files](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-offload-session-data), and data that must survive scale in is [stored off the instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-persist-data-off-instance). Then [they can scale horizontally](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-stateless-scales-horizontally): any instance can serve any request.
takeaway: A stateless tier keeps session data off the instance, so the group can remove any instance.
twin: If the stem said "keeps uploaded files on the local disk of each instance" instead: Amazon S3, because data that must survive scale in is [stored off the instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-persist-data-off-instance).
say: I'd move the sessions to DynamoDB, so any instance can serve any user.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The Region has three Availability Zones. At peak load, the application needs 6 instances. The application must be fault tolerant across multiple Availability Zones: if one zone fails, 6 instances must keep serving requests with no wait for new instances. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: with no wait for new instances

options.text: Keep the minimum capacity at 6 instances, and rely on the group to launch replacement instances in the other zones after a zone fails.
options.why: Replacements arrive [within minutes](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-replacement-time-minutes), so users wait for capacity; that is high availability, not the fault tolerance that the stem asks for.

options.text: Configure the Auto Scaling group and the load balancer to use subnets in three Availability Zones of the Region.
options.why: AWS recommends a group [across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-resilience-practices) with the load balancer in the same zones; three zones keep the spare share small.

options.text: Configure the group to use two Availability Zones, and set the minimum capacity to 12 instances, with 6 in each zone.
options.why: It works, but two zones need six instances each, twelve in all, which costs more than nine instances across three zones.

options.text: Set the minimum capacity of the group to 9 instances, so that each of the three Availability Zones runs 3 instances.
options.why: Nine instances in three zones leave six when one zone fails, so the peak load is served with no launch and no wait.

options.text: Extend the Auto Scaling group into a second AWS Region, and keep 6 instances in each Region behind the same load balancer.
options.why: An Auto Scaling group [can span Availability Zones, but not AWS regions](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-regional-spans-azs-not-regions), so one group cannot extend into a second Region.

explanation: Fault tolerant here means no wait after a zone fails, so the spare capacity runs before the failure. Well-Architected says [static stability is preferred for high availability](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-static-stability-for-az-loss) when a whole zone is lost. Three zones with three instances each still leave six after one zone fails, with the fewest instances.
takeaway: Fault tolerant across zones: size the group so that the remaining zones carry the peak without new launches.
twin: If the stem said "a short wait for new instances is acceptable" instead: six instances across the zones, because the group can [launch instances in another one to compensate](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-az-unavailable-launch-elsewhere).
say: Three zones with three instances each, so losing a zone still leaves six running.
